query: For high-entropy alloys intended as intermediate materials in plasma-facing reactor components, what single intervention could improve heat-transfer capability while preserving structural integrity? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the expected outcome compared with current intermediate-layer performance, the temperature and loading conditions under which it should hold, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a strong crystallographic texture via directional solidification into the high-entropy alloy (HEA) intermediate layer will enhance the heat‐transfer capability by aligning grains for optimal phonon transport along the heat-flux direction, while maintaining its structural integrity under high thermal flux and irradiation.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory HEA intermediate layer (e.g., a BCC‐structured alloy such as (CrFeTiTa)70W30 or a similar variant) produced by conventional mechanical alloying and sintering, which exhibits a random polycrystalline grain orientation and already demonstrated high thermal stability and irradiation resistance.
generation.intervention: Apply a directional solidification process during fabrication to induce a marked crystallographic texture (for example, a <100> preferred orientation) in the HEA intermediate layer.
generation.conditions: The HEA intermediate layer will operate under fusion‐relevant conditions – operating temperatures from approximately 500 °C to 1000 °C, subjected to high heat fluxes and an intense flux of high-energy particles/irradiation.
generation.structural_mediator: The induced grain alignment (texturing) in the single-phase BCC structure, resulting in reduced grain-boundary thermal resistance along the heat-flow direction.
generation.mechanism: A preferred grain orientation enhances lattice phonon group velocities and extends the phonon mean free path along the heat-transfer direction, effectively reducing the thermal boundary resistance. At the same time, the retained phase stability and grain-boundary architecture continue to deliver the required mechanical strength and irradiation tolerance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline randomly oriented HEA intermediate layers, the textured layers will exhibit an improvement of roughly 20% or more in directional thermal conductivity while maintaining similar mechanical and irradiation resistance properties.
generation.baseline: Standard HEA intermediate layers produced via conventional processing (mechanical alloying and sintering) without any texture control, which show adequate but suboptimal heat-transfer performance.
generation.boundary: If the directional processing leads to excessive grain growth or inhomogeneous textures that might compromise mechanical strength or if the induced texture degrades significantly under prolonged high-flux irradiation, the beneficial effect on thermal conductivity may not be sustained.
generation.uncertainty: This hypothesis extrapolates from MD simulation findings on phonon behaviors in CoCrFeNiCu (PMC11369437::web::000::abstract) and interfacial engineering successes in GaN-on-diamond systems (PMC11984094::web::000::abstract). The novelty lies in leveraging texture engineering in HEAs (not previously proposed in the provided map) to improve thermal performance. However, it remains uncertain how well the induced texture will be preserved under the combined stresses of high temperature and irradiation, as seen in related studies such as the temperature-dependent lattice conductivity in MoWTaTiZr alloys (PMC11938135::web::011::effect_of_temperature_on_lattice_thermal).

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of HEA intermediate layer samples: one set using conventional sintering (random grain orientation) and a second set processed by directional solidification to induce a strong <100> texture. Verify the texture using electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD). Subject both sets to high-temperature conditions (500–1000 °C) and simulated irradiation (using ion irradiation) to mimic fusion reactor environments.
measurements: EBSD for quantifying degree and uniformity of texture
Laser flash analysis to measure thermal diffusivity and calculate thermal conductivity along the heat flux direction
Mechanical property evaluations (tensile tests, hardness measurements) before and after irradiation
Microstructural characterization (via SEM/TEM) post-irradiation to assess texture retention and phase stability
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the textured samples do not exhibit at least a 20% improvement in directional thermal conductivity compared to the randomly oriented samples, or if their mechanical and irradiation resistance properties show significant degradation relative to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractHigh entropy alloys (HEAs) are alloys composed of five or more primary elements in equal or nearly equal proportions of atoms. In the present study, the thermophysical properties of the CoCrFeNiCu high entropy alloy (HEA) were investigated by a molecular dynamics (MD) method at nanoscale. The effects of the content of individual elements on lattice thermal conductivity kp were revealed, and the results suggested that adjusting the atomic content can be a way to control the lattice thermal conductivity of HEAs. The effects of temperature on kp were investigated quantitively, and a power-law relationship of kp with T−0.419 was suggested, which agrees with previous findings. The effects of temperature and the content of individual elements on volumetric specific heat capacity Cv were also studied: as the temperature increases, the Cv of all HEAs slightly decreases and then increases. The effects of atomic content on Cv varied with the comprising elements. cited_evidence.text: The lattice thermal conductivity of MoWTaTiZr RHEA exhibited an approximately linear relationship with the reciprocal of temperature. The slope of the fitted line is 124.30. It demonstrates that the lattice thermal conductivity of MoWTaTiZr is determined by the phonon-phonon anharmonic effect. As the temperature increases, according to the Bose-Einstein law, the number of phonons increases significantly, which increases the phonon-phonon scattering rate. The long wavelength behavior decreases with increasing temperature and the anharmonic scattering intensity increases with increasing temperature. Strong chemical disorder reduces the phonon lifetime of the HEA, and strong anharmonic scattering of high-frequency phonons and strong electron-phonon scattering lead to a decrease in the lattice thermal conductivity. AbstractGaN high electron mobility transistors (HEMTs) on SiC substrates are the highest performing commercially available transistors for high-power, high-frequency applications. However, Joule self-heating limits the maximum areal power density, i.e., operating power is derated to ensure the lifetime of GaN-based devices. Diamond is attractive as a heat sink due to its record-high thermal conductivity combined with its high electrical resistivity. GaN-on-diamond devices have been demonstrated, bringing the diamond as close as possible to the active device area. The GaN/diamond interface, close to the channel heat source, needs to efficiently conduct high heat fluxes, but it can present a significant thermal boundary resistance (TBR). In this work, we implement nanoscale trenches between GaN and diamond to explore new strategies for reducing the effective GaN/diamond TBR (TBReff). A 3× reduction in GaN/diamond TBReff was achieved using this approach, which is consistent with the increased contact area; thermal properties were measured using nanosecond transient thermoreflectance (ns-TTR).
